patient.name: Charles Fenwick
patient.chief_complaint: Progressive bilateral foot and leg weakness for 8 months following chemotherapy for multiple myeloma
patient.hpi: Charles Fenwick is a 67-year-old retired professor presenting 8 months post-completion of bortezomib-based chemotherapy for IgG kappa multiple myeloma (achieved complete response). He reports progressive bilateral foot and leg weakness that began during his third cycle of bortezomib and has worsened despite completion of therapy 4 months ago. He has bilateral foot drop and significant difficulty climbing stairs. He also reports severe burning and shooting pain in both hands and feet that he rates 8/10, which interferes with sleep and activities of daily living. His oncologist attributed this to 'expected bortezomib peripheral neuropathy' and started gabapentin 600 mg three times daily with only partial pain relief. However, Charles notes that over the past 6 weeks he has experienced three episodes of sudden severe grip weakness in his right hand lasting 30-60 seconds followed by recovery, which he has not reported to his oncologist as he attributed them to fatigue. He also notes that his symptoms seem to fluctuate — some days much better than others. He has had a repeat serum protein electrophoresis at 2 months post-treatment showing complete response (no M-spike), but his light chain ratio was mildly abnormal at 3.2 (kappa 42 mg/L, lambda 13 mg/L). He denies bowel or bladder dysfunction. His ECOG performance status has deteriorated from 0 at diagnosis to 2 now.
pmh: Multiple myeloma IgG kappa — complete response post-bortezomib/lenalidomide/dexamethasone (VRd) x 8 cycles (completed 4 months ago)

report.summary: ABNORMAL NCS/EMG. TERMINAL SLOWING PATTERN — hallmark of anti-MAG neuropathy. Disproportionately prolonged distal motor latencies (DML) compared to proximal conduction velocities. This pattern is DIFFERENT from pure bortezomib axonal neuropathy. Bortezomib causes length-dependent axonal neuropathy (amplitude loss); anti-MAG causes terminal slowing (DML prolonged, amplitudes preserved relatively). Both may coexist here.

motor.note: DML 9.4 ms (markedly prolonged >4.4 ms); velocity 44.8 m/s (mildly reduced but relatively preserved). DISPROPORTIONATE DML vs velocity = TERMINAL SLOWING — anti-MAG pattern.

motor.nerve: Right Peroneal Motor (ankle to fibular head)
motor.note: DML 9.8 ms (markedly prolonged); velocity 38.4 m/s (mildly slow). Amplitude also reduced — bortezomib axonal loss superimposed.
motor.flag: terminal slowing + amplitude reduction (mixed: anti-MAG + bortezomib)

sensory.flag: reduced amplitude and velocity — both anti-MAG and bortezomib contributing

emg.summary: Chronic axonal loss in distal muscles with relatively preserved recruitment compared to severity of NCS abnormalities. This dissociation (more severe NCS slowing than EMG denervation) is characteristic of anti-MAG terminal slowing — the major dysfunction is at the terminal myelin junction (juxtagranular region), not diffuse axonal loss.

report.overall_impression: ANTI-MAG NEUROPATHY (terminal slowing pattern) SUPERIMPOSED ON BORTEZOMIB AXONAL NEUROPATHY. Two distinct mechanisms: (1) Anti-MAG IgM paraprotein neuropathy — terminal slowing, disproportionate DML prolongation, relatively preserved proximal velocities; (2) Bortezomib-associated axonal neuropathy — amplitude reduction, length-dependent. Treatment implications: anti-MAG does NOT respond to IVIG; first-line is rituximab (anti-CD20). Bortezomib neuropathy: supportive, may improve over time after cessation. Episodic hand weakness may represent transient focal conduction impairment from the anti-MAG process.

report.summary: Bone marrow biopsy: IgG kappa plasma cells <5% (residual myeloma in near-stringent CR — consistent with myeloma monitoring). ADDITIONALLY: small lymphoplasmacytic clone identified — IgM kappa lymphoplasmacytic cells comprising 3% of cellularity. Negative for Waldenstrom's macroglobulinemia (lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma) — <10% threshold not met.
report.flow_cytometry: IgG kappa plasma cells <5% (residual myeloma). Separate IgM kappa clone: 3% lymphoplasmacytic cells — IgM MGUS (<10% = not Waldenstrom's macroglobulinemia).
report.interpretation: Dual hematological findings: (1) IgG kappa myeloma in near-stringent CR (<5% plasma cells), (2) NEW IgM kappa MGUS (3% lymphoplasmacytic cells <10% threshold) — separate clone from the original myeloma. IgM MGUS is producing anti-MAG antibody. This represents BICLONAL GAMMOPATHY (rare — two separate hematological clones). Anti-MAG neuropathy treatment: rituximab (targets IgM B cell/lymphoplasmacytic clone).

results.citation: Léger JM et al. (2013) Intravenous immunoglobulin versus placebo for anti-MAG neuropathy. Cochrane Database Syst Rev.
results.summary: IVIG is NOT recommended for anti-MAG neuropathy — trials show no significant benefit. Rituximab (anti-CD20) is the preferred treatment targeting the IgM-producing B cell clone. Response rate: ~50% partial improvement with rituximab 375 mg/m² x 4 weekly doses.

results.citation: Dalakas MC (2010) Advances in the diagnosis, pathogenesis and treatment of CIDP. Nat Rev Neurol 6:314-324.
results.summary: Anti-MAG neuropathy is distinguished from CIDP by: terminal slowing on NCS (DML disproportionately prolonged vs velocity), IgM paraprotein, anti-MAG antibody; CIDP responds to IVIG/steroids; anti-MAG does not respond to IVIG and requires rituximab.

output.interpretation: IVIG contraindicated as first-line for anti-MAG neuropathy — this is a critical error to avoid. Rituximab 375 mg/m² IV weekly x4 is the standard treatment. Anti-CD20 targets the IgM-producing lymphoplasmacytic clone. Expected timeline: 3-6 months for anti-MAG titer reduction and neurological stabilization. Note: given residual myeloma on lenalidomide maintenance, hematology co-management essential before adding rituximab.

report.summary: Sural nerve biopsy: widely spaced myelin lamellae on EM (characteristic of anti-MAG neuropathy — IgM deposits disrupt the juxtagranular myelin at paranodal/terminal junctions). IgM and complement deposits on immunofluorescence at myelin sheath.
report.histology: Light microscopy: moderately reduced large myelinated fiber density. Axonal degeneration present (bortezomib component). Semi-thin: abnormally wide myelin lamellae in some fibers. Immunofluorescence: IgM deposits at outer myelin loop (juxtagranular region) — PATHOGNOMONIC FOR ANTI-MAG NEUROPATHY. C3d complement deposits co-localizing with IgM. Electron microscopy: widely spaced myelin lamellae ('fluffy' myelin) — the characteristic finding of anti-MAG paranodopathy.
report.interpretation: ANTI-MAG NEUROPATHY confirmed histologically by IgM deposits at myelin with widely spaced lamellae on EM. Axonal degeneration from bortezomib is the secondary component. Rituximab treatment targets the IgM-producing clone.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Anti-MAG neuropathy from IgM MGUS (biclonal with treated IgG kappa myeloma) superimposed on bortezomib-associated axonal neuropathy
critical_actions: Check anti-MAG antibody — terminal slowing on NCS demands anti-MAG workup in any patient with IgM paraprotein
Immunofixation (not just SPEP) — SPEP misses small paraproteins below detection threshold (~0.3 g/dL)
Do NOT use IVIG for anti-MAG neuropathy — it is IVIG-refractory; rituximab is correct treatment
MRI spine to exclude myeloma cord compression (urgent in known myeloma patient with bilateral foot drop)
Bone marrow biopsy to characterize both clones — treatment differs between myeloma and MGUS management
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT use IVIG for anti-MAG neuropathy — clinical trials show no benefit; wastes resources and delays rituximab
Do not attribute entirely to bortezomib — terminal slowing on NCS is not a bortezomib pattern
Do not miss IgM paraprotein by relying on SPEP alone — immunofixation is required for trace paraproteins
Do not restart bortezomib without recognizing that anti-MAG neuropathy is a separate treatable complication

differential.key_distinguishing: Bortezomib causes length-dependent axonal neuropathy (amplitude loss); terminal slowing (disproportionate DML prolongation) is NOT bortezomib's pattern; episodic weakness and fluctuation are not bortezomib features
Anti-MAG neuropathy has distinct NCS terminal slowing vs CIDP patchy conduction block; anti-MAG antibody confirmed; IgM paraprotein present; CIDP responds to IVIG — anti-MAG does not
MRI spine: no cord compression, no leptomeningeal enhancement; SPEP no M-spike (myeloma in remission); the neuropathy is from anti-MAG MGUS, not myeloma recurrence
HbA1c 7.4% contributes background axonal neuropathy; terminal slowing on NCS is NOT diabetic; anti-MAG antibody is the primary driver of demyelinating component

key_reasoning_points: DIAGNOSTIC PUZZLE: Three layers of complexity — (1) bortezomib neuropathy creates anchoring, (2) SPEP shows no M-spike (IgM MGUS below detection), (3) biclonal gammopathy (two separate hematological clones) is rare and unexpected
TERMINAL SLOWING vs AXONAL: Key NCS pattern recognition — bortezomib causes amplitude loss (axonal); anti-MAG causes DML prolongation (terminal demyelination at paranodes)
SPEP BLIND SPOT: SPEP detects M-spikes >0.3 g/dL; small IgM MGUS producing anti-MAG requires immunofixation which is 10-100x more sensitive
IVIG CONTRAINDICATION: Anti-MAG neuropathy is one of the few neuropathies where IVIG is explicitly not recommended — it is CIDP-like on NCS but IVIG-refractory; rituximab is the treatment
EPISODIC WEAKNESS: Transient grip weakness episodes represent focal conduction failure at anti-MAG-disrupted paranodes — not TIA or myeloma-related
BICLONAL GAMMOPATHY: Two simultaneous hematological clones (IgG myeloma + IgM MGUS) is uncommon but recognized; management of each clone requires separate strategies
